title: Ticket Table Solved Each Team Before Comparing
text: id: COMP-011 domain: math title: Ticket Table Solved Each Team Before Comparing tags: table, comparison, tickets memory: A support dashboard question once fooled me because I compared teams before finishing their individual ledgers. I gave Team A its own start, closed, received calculation, then did the same for Team B. Only then did I total and compare. The table made the winner obvious.

title: Ratio Mixture Counted Total Parts Before Liters
text: id: COMP-009 domain: math title: Ratio Mixture Counted Total Parts Before Liters tags: ratio, mixture, parts memory: A mixture ratio felt like two numbers competing until I counted total parts. Two parts and five parts made seven equal chunks of the final volume. I found liters per part first, then multiplied by each side of the ratio. The concentrate and water added back to the requested total.

title: Tiered Pricing Split Base Units Extra Units Fixed Fee
text: id: COMP-001 domain: math title: Tiered Pricing Split Base Units Extra Units Fixed Fee tags: tiered-pricing, units, addition memory: I once answered a tiered utility bill too quickly and charged every unit at the blended-looking rate. The correction was embarrassing because the structure was simple: first tier, extra units, fixed fee. I rewrote it as 100 base units, then units above 100, then the fixed charge. The revised bill matched the invoice exactly, and I remembered how a tier problem punishes shortcuts.

title: Subscription Total Kept Fee And Credit As Separate Signs
text: id: COMP-012 domain: math title: Subscription Total Kept Fee And Credit As Separate Signs tags: money, subscription, credit memory: A subscription total once drifted because I treated a credit like another fee. I wrote monthly cost times months, then setup fee as a plus, then credit as a minus. Seeing the signs separately kept the final price honest. The bill matched when the credit stayed negative.

title: Schedule Times Added Durations Then Rolled Hours
text: id: COMP-008 domain: math title: Schedule Times Added Durations Then Rolled Hours tags: time, schedule, minutes memory: A schedule answer once came out an hour off because I added minutes in my head while crossing noon. I wrote the durations as one total minute count, converted to hours and leftover minutes, then added that to the start time. The clock stopped being slippery once minutes had their own line.
